column3: The repeated conditional wording concerns Lot's response to his people and does not clarify aiding idols or burning Ibrahim.
God's command immediately brings a thing into being, contrasting with idols that require people to act on their behalf.
The people's accusation that Ibrahim acted against their gods begins the same causal test that exposes the gods' helplessness.
This conditional question about a penalty has no meaningful link to the focus ayah.
The introduction to Ibrahim's surrounding narrative supplies only broad prophetic context for the confrontation.
It frames hostility toward prophets alongside God's sufficient guidance and help, broadly illuminating the opposition in the focus.
Its leaders command their people to persist with their gods, directly paralleling the focus command to aid their gods.
Ibrahim's question about the images the people devote themselves to introduces the idolatry contested in the focus.
Pharaoh's accusation against Musa does not illuminate the idolaters' command against Ibrahim.
Noah's people explicitly urge one another not to abandon their named gods, closely paralleling the collective defense of gods.
God's command to the fire directly reverses the attempted burning announced in the focus and protects Ibrahim.
The challenge over why false objects of reliance cannot help one another exposes the failed help claimed for the gods in the focus.
The proposal concerning Yusuf uses the same conditional phrase without bearing on idolatry or Ibrahim.
The group's confidence that it is a mutually victorious body loosely echoes the focus's collective appeal to aid.
It recounts the same response of Ibrahim's people, including the command to burn him and God's rescue from the fire.
The demand for proof of a sectarian claim does not clarify the focus.
The description of the God-fearing follows the same passage but adds little to the attempted defense of idols.
The warning against distraction by wealth and children has no direct relevance to the focus reading.
The conditional statement about divine play does not clarify the command to burn Ibrahim.
Ibrahim's pledge to devise a plan against the idols is the immediate provocation for the command in the focus.
God's promise that His servants will be helped broadly explains the divine reversal of the idolaters' attack.
The disbelievers resent mention of their gods while rejecting the Most Merciful, directly framing their hostility in the same episode.
The outcome of the plot against Ibrahim shows that the people attempting to aid their gods became the greater losers.
The recording of people's deeds does not clarify the focus's contest over divine agency.
This accusation among the condemned lacks a meaningful connection to the focus.
The question rejects desiring gods besides God, reinforcing the false worship challenged in the focus.
Lot's prayer for God's help against corrupters provides a broad counterpoint to seeking help for false gods.
The account of Solomon's judgment and gifts does not illuminate the focus.
The blessed reminder is nearby narrative context but does not directly explain the focus action.
God's action against the elephant army shows a hostile plot being overturned, broadly resembling the defeat of the plot against Ibrahim.
God's promised renewal of creation affirms divine effective action only in a general sense.
Ibrahim's question about worshipping what can neither benefit nor harm gives the theological basis for the gods needing human aid.
Human hands as an instrument of divine punishment do not clarify the idolaters' defense of their gods.
This account of a broken covenant and ensuing hostility is unrelated to the focus.
Ibrahim's ironic instruction to ask the chief idol if it can speak continues the demonstration of the idols' incapacity.
The description of believers performing zakat has no meaningful link to the focus.
The destruction by burning of the calf reverses the focus's attempted burning and demonstrates the fate of a false god.
The question about what people think of the Lord only broadly challenges their mistaken theology.
It denies any protector or helper besides God, directly correcting the misplaced search for aid in the focus.
The mention of fiery punishment for hostile speech and killing offers only a distant fire motif.
God's prior gift of sound judgment to Ibrahim provides immediate context for his challenge to the idols.
The contrast between poets' speech and deeds does not clarify the attempted defense of idols.
The punishment of those who burn believing men and women broadly parallels the persecutory violence threatened in the focus.
Ibrahim's smashing of the idols is the act that leads directly to the people's command to burn him.
The absence of a helper for those cursed by God only generally relates to failed support.
Its destructive fire in a parable is not materially connected to the focus's attempted burning.
The statement about a message for worshippers does not explain the focus.
The failure of patrons to help one another on the Day of Judgment reinforces the limits of creaturely support.
The instruction to harvest a crop has no link to the focus.
God's production of fire from green trees offers only a general contrast between divine provision and human use of fire.
It states that victory comes only from God, countering the focus's appeal to secure victory by aiding idols.
Musa's call to rely on God gives a broad alternative to reliance on false gods.
The people's appeal to inherited idol worship identifies the commitment that motivates their action in the focus.
Musa's admission about a past act does not clarify the focus.
The challenge to return the soul has no direct bearing on the focus.
Ibrahim's rebuke of the people and what they worship immediately precedes their violent response in the focus.
The recording of deeds does not clarify the focus's central reading.
The conditional denial of accountability has no meaningful link to the focus.
The instruction to ask people of knowledge does not illuminate the conflict over idols.
The fulfillment of God's promise as action offers only a general affirmation of effective divine action.
The brothers' confidence in their group does not clarify the focus's aid to gods.
God's command produces its intended result at once, contrasting with idols whose defenders must manufacture their effectiveness.
God always accomplishes what He wills, providing a broad contrast to the powerless gods of the focus.
The people briefly acknowledge their own wrongdoing after Ibrahim's challenge, advancing the same exposure of idolatry.
Ibrahim calls the people and their fathers plainly astray, directly answering their inherited devotion to idols.
God's action against 'Ad gives only a broad pattern of divine judgment against a corrupt people.
The demand to restore forefathers does not illuminate the focus.
The people concede that the idols cannot speak, confirming why they must themselves defend them.
It asks what army could help people apart from the Most Merciful, directly challenging the focus's imagined protective support.
The question about a missing object has no meaningful link to the focus.
The warning of approaching judgment does not explain the command to burn Ibrahim.
Yusuf's reminder of his brothers' past act does not clarify the focus.
The people's insult to a messenger does not specifically illuminate the focus.
The rhetorical question whether they have another god rejects the association of gods that underlies the focus.
It denies any protector or helper besides God, correcting the focus's appeal to aid false gods.
The challenge to avert death concerns a separate claim of protection.
The people's uncertainty whether Ibrahim is serious is part of the immediate exchange that precipitates their response in the focus.
The distinction between God's unanswerable action and human accountability broadly clarifies the focus's conflict over agency.
The challenge to summon witnesses besides God loosely parallels seeking outside support for a false claim.
Solomon's command over the wind does not clarify the focus.
It denies any protector or helper besides God, directly opposing reliance on any rival source of aid.
It presents people as helpers of God and His messenger, sharply contrasting rightful service with the focus's effort to help powerless gods.
The failure of both a people's scheme and outside help broadly anticipates the collapse of the plot in the Ibrahim narrative.
The lack of helpers for wrongdoers only generally resonates with failed support.
The calf's place in Israel's hearts supplies a distant example of attachment to a false object of worship.
Ibrahim names the Creator as the true Lord of heaven and earth, directly countering the idols the people seek to defend.
The expectation of an impending calamity does not illuminate the focus.
It presents Ibrahim as a non-polytheist, providing a broad corrective to the idolatry opposed in the focus.
The mortality of messengers does not clarify the focus.
The people's search for whoever acted against their gods openly shows that the gods need human defenders, directly preparing the focus command.
The grading of deeds does not clarify the focus.
Recompense for deeds has no direct link to the focus reading.
The warning against obeying disbelievers is unrelated to aiding idols or the fire.
Believers' mutual shelter and support provide a broad positive contrast to the focus's misplaced collective support for idols.
The command to avoid marital injustice has no meaningful link to the focus.
Helping God and His messengers defines faithful aid, directly contrasting with the focus's call to aid false gods.
The diversity of human striving does not clarify the focus.
The legal warning that rejects certain protectors and helpers has only a distant connection to the focus's appeal for aid.
The family-law instructions do not illuminate the focus.
It explicitly asks why adopted gods failed to help in need, directly exposing the false rescue logic behind aiding idols.
The people identify Ibrahim as the young man who spoke against their gods, immediately advancing the accusation that leads to the focus command.
Their order to bring Ibrahim before the people sets the public confrontation that culminates in the attempted burning.
God's rescue of Ibrahim and Lot supplies the broader outcome of the failed attack announced in the focus.
Ibrahim's question to his father about taking idols as gods directly anticipates his opposition to idolatry in the focus narrative.
It asks whether people associate with God things that create nothing and are themselves created, exposing the incapacity of the gods being defended.
It explicitly says the associated beings cannot help their worshippers or help themselves, directly clarifying why human aid to gods is inverted.
It states that those invoked besides God cannot help their worshippers, directly contradicting the call to aid gods.
It rejects worship of beings that neither harm nor benefit, the same premise Ibrahim uses against the idols in his exchange.
It portrays calls to others besides God as unanswered and futile, reinforcing the helplessness of the gods for whom the people act.
Ibrahim's prayer to be kept from worshipping idols provides a direct thematic contrast to the people's devotion in the focus.
The beings invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created, directly undermining their claim to divinity.
It denies that beings besides God possess provision or power, clarifying the powerlessness of the gods the people try to defend.
Those called besides God cannot remove or transfer harm, broadly reinforcing Ibrahim's exposure of powerless objects of worship.
The demand for proof of gods besides God directly challenges the unsupported association behind the focus.
Ibrahim asks why his father worships what neither hears, sees, nor benefits him, directly articulating the idol critique enacted in the focus.
The Samaritan's calf is presented as a false god, offering another concrete case of a manufactured object falsely treated as divine.
The calf cannot speak or control harm or benefit, directly confirming the incapacity that makes human defense of a god absurd.
Those invoked besides God cannot create even a fly or recover what it takes, strongly exposing the weakness of false gods.
The alleged gods neither create nor control harm, benefit, death, life, or resurrection, directly refuting the status claimed for the focus's idols.
Ibrahim asks his people what they worship, beginning another account of the same confrontation with idolatry.
The people answer that they worship idols and remain devoted to them, closely paralleling the commitment that drives the focus command.
Ibrahim asks whether the idols hear when invoked, directly testing their supposed divine agency.
He asks whether the idols benefit or harm, directly matching the incapacity argument in the surrounding focus narrative.
The appeal to ancestral practice identifies the inherited attachment to idols that also appears among Ibrahim's opponents.
Ibrahim tells his people that they worship idols and fabricate falsehood, directly characterizing the false worship behind the focus.
It says people take gods besides God in hope that they will be helped, directly paralleling the focus's imagined aid through false gods.
The gods cannot help their worshippers, while the worshippers stand as troops for them, precisely reversing the expected protector-protected relation in the focus.
Ibrahim asks what false gods his people desire besides God, directly framing the idolatry opposed in the focus.
Ibrahim addresses the idols as unable even to eat, continuing the demonstration of their inertness.
He asks why the idols do not speak, directly paralleling the challenge in the immediate 21 narrative.
Ibrahim strikes the idols, recounting the same provocative act that brings the attempt to burn him.
The rebuke for worshipping what people themselves carve directly exposes the makers' superiority over their supposed gods.
The people order a construction for a fire and throw Ibrahim into it, a direct parallel to the focus command to burn him.
Their plot against Ibrahim is defeated by God, supplying the same reversal that follows the focus.
After affirming God as Creator, the verse asks whether invoked beings can remove harm or withhold mercy, directly denying their effective agency.
Ibrahim declares himself free of what his father and people worship, directly opposing the shared idol devotion in the focus.
His exception for the One who created him specifies the true divine source against the false gods of the preceding declaration.
The challenge asks what alleged partners have created or share in, directly testing the divine claim of the gods defended in the focus.
No one is more astray than one who calls on beings besides God that cannot answer, directly exposing failed reliance on false gods.
At the gathering, the invoked beings become enemies of their worshippers and reject their worship, completing the failure of their supposed alliance.
The naming of the major goddesses introduces another direct Qur'anic challenge to the gods people set alongside God.
The alleged deities are only names invented by people and their forefathers, directly challenging the human construction of false divine authority.
Ibrahim and those with him disavow both their people and what they worship besides God, extending the focus's rejection of idolatry into a model stance.
The challenge to produce proof for gods besides God directly contests the association that causes the people to defend their idols.
The universal prophetic proclamation that there is no god but God supplies the categorical correction to the focus's plural gods.
The question of who can protect people from God denies any independent protective power to the rivals they invoke.
It declares that worshippers and what they worship besides God will enter Hell, directly denying the idols' capacity to save their defenders.
If the worshipped beings were truly gods, they would not enter Hell, directly applying a decisive test to their claimed divinity.
Calling on another god without proof is condemned, directly rejecting the unsupported divine claim behind the focus's idols.
Ibrahim asks his people to consider the objects they and their forefathers have worshipped, continuing the direct examination of inherited idolatry.
He calls those worshipped objects his enemies except for the Lord of the worlds, directly reversing the loyalty shown to idols in the focus.
The people tie their idolatry to mutual worldly affection, while the coming judgment leaves them with neither denial nor help, exposing the fragility of their alliance.
Those called besides God possess nothing in the heavens or earth and have no share or supporting role, directly denying the gods' power to assist.
Those invoked besides God do not hear prayer, cannot answer it, and will reject the worship at judgment, directly exposing the failure of their supposed alliance.
If the Most Merciful intends harm, the intercession of gods besides Him cannot help or save, directly answering the focus's appeal to aid gods.
God created both the people and what they make, directly overturning the assumption that a human-made idol could be divine.
The claim that other worshipped beings merely bring people nearer to God exposes a common rationale for the rival-god devotion represented in the focus.
All intercession belongs to God, denying any independent mediation by the gods for whom the people act.
